title: Find the target
blurb: This cancer cell's division program is in overdrive. Pick ONE protein to block.

brief.simple: The K562 cancer cell keeps dividing. You get **one move**: switch off one gene or add one drug. Try to pull the **cell division** bar down to the black goal mark. Explore first! The Explore and Playground pages are open to you.
brief.student: Choose **one** knockdown or drug that lowers K562's **cell-division program** to the goal. Tip: test candidates in the Playground first, just as scientists test targets before committing to a drug program.
brief.deep: Single-perturbation target selection on the mitotic program score (scaled). Measured knockdowns dominate; drug approximations are lower confidence.

hints: Growth master switches that feed division are good places to look.
Try MTOR, RPTOR or SIRT7, or the drug everolimus.
A gentler, more specific choice: CDK6 (the target of palbociclib).

debrief.simple: Real scientists do this with experiments like the ones in this app: switch off thousands of genes, one at a time, and see which ones the cancer needs. But a good target also has to be **safe**. Many genes that slow cancer cells also slow healthy cells. Try the **Do no harm** mission next!
debrief.student: Genome-scale CRISPR screens like Replogle et al.'s are used to find genes a cancer depends on. [@replogle2022] The strongest hits here (MTOR, RPTOR, SIRT7) are 'core essential': they matter to almost every cell. That makes them poor drug targets unless the cancer depends on them more than normal tissue does.
debrief.deep: Strong transcriptional phenotypes often reflect pan-essential genes (ribosome biogenesis, mTORC1). Prioritization requires a differential dependency between tumor and normal cells, plus druggability, which is the motivation for comparing K562 to RPE1. [@replogle2022] [@hughes2011]
